question: v14
q: My power bill in Perth feels huge. Is that just me?

transcript.answer:
You're not imagining a bigger bill, but the price of electricity in Perth has barely moved. What's changed is that the government rebates have stopped.

**The Perth electricity tariff is up only about 2.4% in a year**
- Perth electricity prices rose **2.4% in the year to August 2026** (ABS monthly CPI). Since 2023 they've gone up about 2.5% each July: the price index went from 95.2 to 97.6, then 100.0, then 102.4.
- Across Australia, electricity prices rose **13.2% over the same year**. Over the three years from June 2023 to August 2026, Perth's underlying price rose about **10%**, compared with about **21%** nationally. So Perth has done relatively well on the price itself.

**Why the bill still feels huge: the rebates have run out**
The CPI counts state and federal energy bill credits as price cuts. That's why Perth's figures swing wildly, from –50% to +289% year on year. Looking at the Perth electricity price index (100 = full price, no credit):

| Period | Index | What it means |
|---|---|---|
| Aug 2024 – Feb 2025 | about 26–50 | Large credits wiped out most of the bill |
| Oct 2025 – Jan 2026 | about 69–90 | Smaller credits |
| Feb 2026 onward | 100 → 102.4 | No credits: you pay the full bill |

So if your last bill or two had a credit on them, today's bill can look several times bigger even though the tariff has only gone up a few per cent. Two other things may be adding to it:
- **How much power you use.** Heating or cooling in heavy-use seasons pushes the bill up, and the CPI doesn't measure this because it tracks prices, not usage.
- **General cost of living.** Overall inflation in Perth was **4.3% in August 2026**, a bit above the national **4.0%**, so other costs are adding to the pressure too.

**In short:** it's not just you. Every Perth household has lost its bill credits since early 2026. But the actual price of electricity there is up only about 2.4% in the past year, well below the national rise of 13%. Comparing your kWh usage with the same bill last year should show whether usage is also part of the jump.
